passage:
Meher: ok who's got news
Asif: you didn't hear it from me but Zeenat likes Arjun from 10-B 😅
Meher: NO WAY
Kabir: since when??
Asif: she wrote Arjun's name on her geometry box, I saw
Meher: I can't, that's so good
Kabir: Asif always knows everything
Asif: what can I say 😊

Zeenat was offline. A minute later Asif remembered telling Kabir about Meher's failed maths test last week. His stomach dipped. He wondered what they said about him when he left the chat. He typed, “anyway, don't say anything to her.”

Nobody replied.

qa.q: Whose name did Zeenat write on her geometry box?
qa.a: Zeenat wrote Arjun's name on her geometry box.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling when remembering the gossip about Meher's maths test?
qa.a: Asif felt a nervous dip, worrying that the chat might be talking about Asif when Asif left.

qa.q: What choice did Asif make after the stomach dipped?
qa.a: Asif typed a request to not say anything to Zeenat, though nobody replied.

qa.q: How might Zeenat feel if learning that the chat knew about the name on her geometry box?
qa.a: Zeenat may feel embarrassed and betrayed, since a private crush became entertainment before Zeenat could share it.

grounding: A teenager gossips about a peer's crush to bond with the group and gain status, and feels a nervous thought that they might be next.

passage:
On the school bus from the kasba, the back seat was the place to be. Ritu leaned in as the bus rattled over the bridge. “Did you hear? Yamini sent the wrong note. It was meant for Sumit, and it went to Sir!” The girls shrieked. Ritu enjoyed being at the centre; everyone was looking at her, waiting for the next line. Nobody asked how she knew.

Somebody said, “Poor Yamini, though.” Ritu laughed it off. But as the bus turned at the market, a thought crept in. What do they say about me when I get off first? She watched her own stop go by, and stayed seated a little longer than she needed.

qa.q: Who did the note go to by mistake?
qa.a: The note meant for Sumit went to Sir.

qa.q: Why did Ritu stay seated a little longer than needed?
qa.a: Ritu felt a nervous thought that the others might gossip about Ritu after getting off, so leaving felt risky.

qa.q: What choice did Ritu make when someone said, “Poor Yamini, though”?
qa.a: Ritu laughed it off instead of stopping the story.

qa.q: What might Yamini feel on hearing the bus story the next day?
qa.a: Yamini would likely feel mortified and exposed, wondering who told and who else knows.

grounding: A teenager tells a peer's mistake on a bus to bond with the group and gain status, then feels the nervous thought of being the next topic.

passage:
Monday: At the back of the school bus, Thomas said, “Guess who's been writing Priya's name in his rough book? Jeevan!” The group howled. Kunal slapped his back. Thomas felt ten feet tall.
Wednesday: Thomas had another story, this time about Jeevan failing the maths unit test. More laughter. The seniors even moved over to make space for him on the back seat. He liked it there.
The next Monday: Walking into class, Thomas heard two girls whisper and stop when he came near. His stomach tightened. What were they saying? Had someone seen his own test? He sat down, pretending to read, ears burning, and noticed Jeevan sitting alone by the window.

qa.q: What did Thomas say Jeevan had been writing?
qa.a: He said Jeevan had been writing Priya's name in his rough book.

qa.q: What was Thomas feeling when the two girls stopped whispering?
qa.a: He felt anxious and nervous that he might be the next topic, his stomach tightening and ears burning.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could Thomas do now?
qa.a: He gained status by gossiping about Jeevan; now he could stop sharing stories and quietly say sorry to Jeevan.

qa.q: How might Jeevan be feeling sitting alone by the window?
qa.a: He probably feels embarrassed and isolated, his crush and his test results turned into jokes.

grounding: Shows a teenager gossiping about a peer's crush and marks to bond with the group and gain status, then fearing he's the next topic.

passage:
Kamal, you asked why I never join gossip at family functions. Let me tell you. This is your Lalremsiami aunty, from when I was fourteen in Aizawl.
There was a girl in our class, Mawii, who failed her English test. I found out and told our group at lunch. “Mawii got four out of twenty!” Everyone laughed. The popular girls asked me to sit with them after that.
Oh, I loved it. Every week I had some new story, and every week I had a better seat.
But I also lay awake some nights, wondering what they said about me when I wasn't there. Every time a group went quiet as I walked up, my heart jumped.
Mawii changed schools the next year. I've never forgotten her face at that lunch.

qa.q: What mark did Mawii get?
qa.a: Four out of twenty.

qa.q: How did young Lalremsiami feel about her new seat, and at night?
qa.a: She loved the status and attention, but at night felt anxious and uneasy, wondering what others said about her.

qa.q: At what point in the story could Lalremsiami have made a different choice?
qa.a: When she first found out about Mawii's test, she could have kept it to herself instead of trading it for a seat.

qa.q: How might Mawii have felt at that lunch?
qa.a: She likely felt humiliated and exposed, with the whole group laughing at her marks.

grounding: An elder recalls gossiping about a classmate's failed test to gain status in a group, enjoying it while fearing she'd be next.

passage:
The school trip bus was stuck in traffic for three hours on the ghat road, hot and noisy, with nothing to do. Ankita's row was bored.
“Did you see Jaya forget her lines in the play?” Ankita whispered. “She just stood there, mouth open, like a fish.” The girls burst out laughing. Someone passed her a packet of chips as a reward. Ankita felt warm, liked, at the centre.
She told another story, and another. The row got louder.
Then, in a quiet moment, she heard a laugh from the row behind, and her own name. She froze. What were they saying? She pulled her knees up and stared at the window. Jaya, two rows ahead, had her headphones on and hadn't turned once.

qa.q: How long was the bus stuck in traffic?
qa.a: For three hours on the ghat road.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she heard her own name?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, worried she was now the topic of someone else's laughter.

qa.q: What would you advise Ankita to do on the rest of the trip?
qa.a: She could stop the stories about Jaya, change the topic to a game, and maybe say sorry to Jaya later.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt, keeping her headphones on?
qa.a: She may have felt hurt and embarrassed, perhaps guessing she was being laughed at and shutting it out.

grounding: Shows a teenager gossiping about a classmate's mistake on a long trip to gain status, then nervously hearing her own name.

passage:
On the steps outside the Chennai coaching centre, Indu leaned in. "Guess who writes Arvind's name in the back of her rough book? Meena." Kavitha shrieked; Divya covered her mouth. For five whole minutes Indu was the centre of the circle, adding details: the little hearts, the way Meena went red in chemistry. It felt warm, being the one who knew things.
Then Meena herself walked past with her bag. The circle went silent, then burst into giggles. Meena looked at them, puzzled, and walked faster.
On the bus home, Indu scrolled through her phone. Kavitha had already sent "Meena + Arvind" to someone else. Indu stared at it. If they could pass on Meena's rough book this fast, what would they do with her own diary, the one Kavitha had flipped through last week?

qa.q: Whose name did Meena write in the back of her rough book?
qa.a: Arvind's name.

qa.q: What was Indu feeling on the bus home?
qa.a: Indu felt a nervous unease, worried the group might one day spread her own secrets just as fast.

qa.q: What could Indu do next time the group wants juicy news?
qa.a: Change the subject or keep other people's private things private, even if it means not being the centre of the circle.

qa.q: What was it like for Meena walking past the giggling circle?
qa.a: Meena felt puzzled and uncomfortable, sensing she was being laughed at without knowing why.

grounding: Shows a teenager gossiping about a peer's crush to bond with friends and gain status, enjoying it while fearing she could be next.
